prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: And, Because, Seven

outputs.L1:
I am going to say what love signifies.

My grandfather said it was the desire of the “I” for another “I,”  
and since then I began to search for you.

My father said the number of love was seven,  
because creation lasted seven days—  
seven days making love to its seven nights.

I looked for you in every seven that ciphered my life,  
and I found you slipping away into other numbers.

One confuses oneself with one’s other self  
when two bodies intertwine in bed.

Three loves have been in my life;  
four it will be when you have left;  
five days that I cannot stand you;  
six kisses in La Paz Centro;  
seven years of not finding you.

Love, show me, from one to a thousand, your nights.

“What is your philosophy of love?” you ask me in bed,  
and I respond:

“It is not a flower—  
but perhaps it is a number.  
Here, I give it to you.  
Hide it between your legs.  
At the count of two,  
make sure it does not fall:

One: Open Sesame.  
Two: Loves have entered your kingdom.”

Translated from the Spanish.
outputs.L2:
I will tell you what love means.

My grandfather claimed it was the longing of one “I” for another “I.”  
From that moment on, I started looking for you.

My father said love’s number was seven,  
because the world was made in seven days—  
seven days making love to their seven nights.

I searched for you inside every seven that encoded my life,  
but I discovered you escaping toward other numbers.

A person mistakes oneself for one’s other self  
when two bodies become tangled together in bed.

There have been three loves in my life.  
There will be four once you are gone.  
Five days have passed in which I cannot bear you.  
Six kisses in La Paz Centro.  
Seven years without finding you.

Love, reveal to me your nights,  
from one all the way to a thousand.

“What is your philosophy of love?” you ask me in bed.  
And I answer:  
It is not a flower—perhaps it is a number.  
Here, I give it to you.  
Hide it between your legs.

When I count to two,  
be careful not to let it drop:

One: Open Sesame.  
Two: Loves have entered your kingdom.

Translated from the Spanish.
outputs.L3:
The speaker presents love as a search for another self, drawing on their grandfather’s definition of love as “the desire to find oneself in another.” This idea gives the poem its central movement: love is not simply affection or attraction, but a longing for recognition, reflection, and completion. The beloved becomes a possible mirror, someone through whom the speaker hopes to encounter a hidden or fuller version of the self.

The poem develops this exploration by linking love to numbers, especially the number seven. Seven carries symbolic weight: it suggests creation, sacred time, cycles, mystery, and completion. Through this number, love becomes connected to the structure of the universe itself, as if desire follows an ancient pattern or rhythm. At the same time, seven also represents longing, because it points toward something that feels meaningful but remains difficult to possess or fully understand.

Throughout the poem, love is portrayed as elusive. Whenever the speaker tries to define or grasp the beloved, the beloved seems to slip away into other meanings, images, and experiences. Love resists being fixed. It is not stable enough to become a simple definition, nor is the beloved reducible to one identity. Instead, desire keeps transforming, leading the speaker from one association to another. This creates a sense that love is always in motion, always just beyond reach.

Physical intimacy is described in language that is both mystical and mathematical. Bodies are not presented merely as physical objects; they become part of a larger symbolic system in which numbers, desire, and sensation are intertwined. Touch becomes a kind of equation, and erotic experience becomes a way of approaching mystery. The poem suggests that intimacy can be both deeply sensual and strangely abstract, joining flesh with thought, pleasure with pattern, and longing with calculation.

In the end, the speaker suggests that love may not be best understood as a flower, a romantic symbol, or a philosophy, an intellectual system. Instead, love may be a number: something precise yet mysterious, abstract yet intimate. Offered as a sensual gift, the number becomes a way of expressing desire beyond ordinary language. Love, then, is not fully explained or resolved; it remains a charged symbol, both embodied and infinite, given from one person to another.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents love as a shifting and elusive force, something that cannot be contained by a single definition or image. Rather than describing love in simple romantic terms, the speaker moves through different ways of understanding it: inherited ideas, personal memories, sensory impressions, and abstract numerical patterns. This movement suggests that love is not stable or easily explained. It changes depending on who is naming it, remembering it, or experiencing it.

At the beginning, the speaker seems to rely on definitions that have been passed down from others. These inherited meanings show how love is often shaped by language, culture, family, and tradition before it is ever personally understood. However, the poem does not fully accept these definitions. Instead, it tests them against memory and lived experience. The speaker’s own recollections make love feel more intimate, physical, and uncertain. Love becomes connected not only to emotion, but also to the body, desire, and the strange ways memory preserves certain moments while losing others.

The poem’s use of numerical imagery further complicates the idea of love. Numbers usually suggest order, logic, and precision, but here they seem to create mystery rather than clarity. By comparing love to a number or code, the poem implies that love may have a hidden structure, but not one that can be easily solved. It can be counted, repeated, or arranged, yet it still escapes full understanding. This makes love feel both mathematical and sensual, both abstract and deeply human.

By the end, the poem moves away from conventional romantic symbols and toward a more complex vision of love. Love is not simply a rose, a promise, or an idealized feeling. It is closer to a code: something patterned but secret, meaningful but difficult to translate. The conclusion suggests that love’s power lies in its refusal to stay fixed. It remains mysterious because it is always changing, always slipping beyond the definitions people try to give it. In this way, the poem portrays love as a force that is intimate, unknowable, and endlessly open to reinterpretation.
outputs.L5:
Seven is a special number because it often appears in stories, nature, and everyday life. There are seven days in a week, and many people use them to plan their work, rest, and time with family. In stories, seven can make things feel magical or important, such as seven heroes, seven mountains, or seven wishes.

Because seven is easy to remember, it is often used in lists and traditions. People may choose it as a lucky number, and it can represent balance, mystery, or completion. And while it is only one number, seven has a strong place in language, culture, and imagination.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem in the style of a Latin American love poem where the speaker explains love through numbers, family sayings, and sensual imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
When my grandmother counted blessings  
she never began with one.

She said, primero, the door must open,  
then the kettle must sing,  
then a hand must find another hand  
in the blue steam of morning.

So I learned arithmetic from kitchens:  
two spoons in the sugar,  
three limes split like small green moons,  
four cousins laughing in the patio  
until the mango tree shook loose its gold.

And you—  
you arrived like the number after hunger,  
the sum no schoolmaster could chalk straight.

My aunt used to say,  
amor que no se dice, se quema,  
love not spoken burns.  
So I speak you:

in the curve of a seven  
I see your shoulder turning away from sleep,  
in the zero, your mouth  
before it becomes a kiss,  
in the eight, two bodies  
learning the dark’s slow multiplication.

What is love?

It is not simple addition, mi vida.  
It is beans swelling overnight  
in a clay bowl.  
It is the debt forgiven  
because blood is blood  
and Sunday is Sunday.  
It is my mother’s warning—  
no cuentes las estrellas,  
don’t count the stars,  
or dawn will find you empty-handed.

But I counted anyway.

I counted the freckles on your back  
like islands after rain,  
the salt at your throat,  
the minutes between your breath and mine.  
I counted until numbers softened,  
until nine became a garden,  
until ten was only the sound  
of your name crossing the room.

Our love has fractions too:  
half a guava shared at the bus stop,  
a quarter moon caught in your hair,  
my whole heart divided  
and still increasing.

Tell me, who taught the orange  
to measure sweetness?  
Who told the river  
how many bends before the sea?

My grandfather said,  
el que ama, espera—  
the one who loves, waits.

So I wait in the warm dusk  
with my shirt open to the wind,  
with the scent of coffee, rain, and your skin  
gathering around me  
like a crowd of ancestors.

And when you come,  
the house becomes an abacus of light:  
each window a bead,  
each breath a bead,  
each kiss sliding  
from this world  
into the next.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

**I’m going to say what love signifies**  
not as my grandfather said it,  
with his hand on the gate of the old house,  
nor as my father said it,  
counting the years on his fingers  
until the number seven became a prayer.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a prose-poem monologue answering “What is your philosophy of love?” using counting from one to seven, references to La Paz Centro, and an intimate bedroom setting.
counterfactuals.output:
One: I believe love begins as a room we are not afraid to enter. Tonight it is this bedroom, the sheet wrinkled like a small white country between us, the lamp making honey of the walls, your breathing the softest weather I know.

Two: Love is not possession. It is the open window. It is letting the night come in with its insects, its far dogs, its scent of dust and warm rain, as if La Paz Centro itself had leaned its forehead against the screen and whispered, remember where you are from, remember what survives heat.

Three: Love is attention. The way I learn the map of your shoulder in the dark. The way silence changes when you are inside it. The way a glass of water on the bedside table becomes holy because your lips have touched it.

Four: Love is labor, but not the labor of chains. More like carrying water. More like sweeping the same floor each morning though the earth keeps returning. In La Paz Centro, the streets know this: ash, sun, hoofprint, market cry, church bell, then again ash, sun, hoofprint. To love is to return without resentment.

Five: Love is not always peace. Sometimes it is the volcano sleeping under the tongue. Sometimes it is the argument folded carefully beside the pillow, neither of us yet brave enough to wear it. But even then, I want my anger to have a door. I want your sorrow to have a chair. I want us to leave the light on.

Six: Love is the body saying yes to being mortal. Your hand on my chest, my hand at your waist, both of us listening for the animal inside the other, the one that fears abandonment, thunder, old grief, the sudden absence of warmth. Here, in this bed, I understand devotion as a blanket pulled over two shivering histories.

Seven: My philosophy of love is this: choose, and choose again. Not blindly. Not obediently. Choose with your eyes open to the cracks in the ceiling, to the laundry waiting, to the names of the dead, to the long road back to La Paz Centro, where the evening turns blue and the houses hold their heat after sunset. Love is not the cure for loneliness; it is the candle we carry into it. It does not say, you will never suffer. It says, when suffering comes, I will know your face in the dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poetic English text that feels translated from Spanish, mixing numerology, desire, and erotic metaphor, with lines about hiding love between someone’s legs and counting “One / Open Sesame. / Two.”
counterfactuals.output:
One.  
Open Sesame.  
Two.

I count the doors of your body  
as if each number were a saint  
with a mouth full of candles.

Three: the fever.  
Four: the moon divided in my hands.  
Five: your name,  
a red fruit I cannot finish saying.

I come from the country of omens,  
where desire is written in salt  
and every kiss has its mathematics.

Let me hide my love between your legs,  
not as a thief hides gold,  
but as the earth hides water—  
deep, trembling, necessary.

Six: the bed becomes a church  
without forgiveness.  
Seven: your laughter unlocks the dark.  
Eight: we are two serpents  
inventing the same circle.

And if the night asks for proof,  
I will give it your shadow,  
your pulse,  
the small arithmetic of our hunger.

Nine: I lose myself.  
Ten: I begin again.

One.  
Open Sesame.  
Two.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
